html:
Jainism is an Indian religion that teaches liberation of the soul through non-violence and self-discipline. Its present form goes back to Mahavira, a teacher of the Ganges plain who lived at about the same time as the Buddha, around the 5th century BCE. Jains see him as the 24th and last of the tirthankaras, the great teachers of their faith.

Its main ideas:

  • Ahimsa: do no harm to any living being, down to insects. Jain monks sweep the path ahead of them, and Jains keep a strict vegetarian diet.
  • Every soul is bound by karma, pictured as fine matter that clings to it. Fasting, self-control and right conduct free it.
  • Truth has many sides, and no one view holds all of it.
  • Non-attachment to possessions.

Monks and nuns lead the way; lay people support them. Two main branches split early: the Digambara, whose monks go naked, and the Shvetambara, who wear white.

Tradition says the emperor Chandragupta Maurya became a Jain monk in his last years. Kings and ministers paid for great Jain works: the Western Gangas put up the giant statue at Shravanabelagola, the Chaulukyas of Gujarat backed the marble temples of Mount Abu, and a Jain council at Valabhi, later the capital of the Maitrakas, wrote down the Shvetambara scriptures. Several of the Khajuraho temples are Jain. Today there are some four to five million Jains, many of them traders, and their teaching of non-violence helped shape Mahatma Gandhi.
